title: MB9-18346
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss the appeal.
The appellant XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Haiti.

The appellant claims that he fears being killed or mistreated in Haiti by several gangs in Cité Soleil, and in particular by two gang leaders whom he calls XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX. He fears for his life because he allegedly fired XXXX XXXX brother and refused to hire people recommended by Cité Soleil's gang leaders for the shelter project carried out as part of the United Nations Office for Project Services' (UNOPS) operations.
Fearing for his life, the appellant left Haiti in 2013 for the United States. He returned to the United States. He entered Canada and filed his refugee protection claim on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017.
On June 13, 2019, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the claim on the grounds that the appellant was not credible on central elements of his claim.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in determining that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
The appellant submits four new documents.

Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (the Act), I can only allow evidence: i. that arose after the RPD rendered its decision; ii. that was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented to the RPD before the decision was rendered.
If the evidence fulfills one or more of these requirements, I must decide whether the evidence is new, credible and relevant before admitting it.2

The appellant's representative submits three new documents and the appellant's affidavit. According to the appellant, these documents show that people want to hurt him and that they are looking for him.

The first document, which is entitled [translation] "lease agreement," is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. I note that this document is almost illegible. The document predates the RPD's decision and contains information about incidents before that decision. After reading the contents of the lease agreement, I find that the document deals with a lease signed on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. In other words, these are not events that arose after the rejection of the refugee protection claim, but rather circumstances that were known before the decision to reject dated June 13, 2019. At all times before the rejection of the refugee protection claim, the appellant could have informed the RPD that he had such a document in his possession, but he failed to do so. The appellant provides no explanation as to why this document was not reasonably available or why he could not reasonably have been expected to file it in the circumstances, before the decision was rendered.

For these reasons, I am of the view that this document does not comply with the requirements set out in subsection 110(4) of the Act because it does not refer to incidents that arose after the RPD's rejection of the refugee protection claim, and it was normally accessible to the appellant, who could have presented it to the RPD in the circumstances at the time the RPD rejected the refugee protection claim. Since it does not comply with the requirements of the Act, I am not required to address the relevance or credibility of this document. Consequently, the evidence is not accepted.

Despite the fact that those three other documents are dated after the date on which the RPD decision was signed, and thus comply with the wording of subsection 110(4) regarding the deadline, and despite the fact that they arose after the rejection of the claim, they fail the jurisprudential analysis test in Singh.

Let us analyze the content of each of the documents submitted. The first document, a medical certificate from the XXXX Hospital, includes numerous spelling mistakes. I note that several accents are missing and that on the certificate's header, it is written 'Hospital' and not 'Hôpital' and that it states "phone" whereas the official languages of Haiti are French and Creole. I also note that all the accents are missing, including the diaeresis on Haïti, and that the word thoracique is spelled 'toraxique' and is also missing an s at the end. I would have expected the medical words to be written by the medical specialist and the document to be written in one of the country's official languages. I also note that the document is not signed. Thus, looking at the medical certificate itself, I find this document not credible.

The second document is a complaint to Haiti's national police, which almost reiterates the content of his attestation. This document states that the authorities went to XXXX XXXX residence and that three men showed up at her home and beat her, asking where the appellant was. They also allegedly threatened her and vandalized her house before leaving. In light of the medical certificate's lack of credibility, I am of the opinion that this document is not credible in terms of its content and therefore not relevant.

The affidavit presented by the appellant is not admissible as new evidence since the affidavit is nothing more than a reiteration of the memorandum filed and does not shed additional new, relevant and credible light on the debate raised before the RPD. Consequently, it is not admissible.
For these reasons, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) finds that these four documents are not admissible as evidence under subsection 110(4) of the Act.
My role is to review all the evidence and to determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.3 The determinative issue is credibility.

The appellant alleges that the RPD erred in fact and in law in that the reasons given by the Board are unreasonable, unsupported by the evidence and constitute errors of law. The appellant alleges several principles of law, but does not provide a full explanation as to why the findings are problematic or what specific errors he has identified in the decision. Rather, the appellant alleges the following: • The RPD based its decision on irrelevant and non-determinative elements for the outcome of the appellant's claimed rights. • The RPD draws negative inferences on elements that are non-determinative and even less relevant to the appellant's claim. • The RPD does not seem to clearly establish what the relevant elements of this case are and what probative value to give to them. • The RPD does not clearly establish how it concludes that there is no risk of persecution, with respect to the fear of being killed or seriously injured in Haiti. • The RPD's decision lacks consistency and intelligibility. • The RPD should not have referred to certain pieces of evidence that support its conclusions, without also referring to contrary evidence. Moreover, the assessment of all the evidence implies that it must be weighed as a whole and not some of it considered in isolation from the rest of the evidence. • The appellant's testimony does not present any contradictions on crucial facts forming the basis of the refugee protection claim. • The RPD erred in its assessment of facts and did not take into account all the evidence provided. • The RPD erred in its assessment of the risks the appellant faces should he leave Canada, and they are unfounded given the violent situation in Haiti. • The RPD erred in a notable and obvious manner in its assessment of the facts and evidence on the record. • The RPD erred with respect to the appellant's lack of subjective fear and the lack of prospective risk. However, the objective risk of threat to the appellant's life that emerges from the documentary evidence and supports the appellant's testimony is sufficient to determine that the RPD's findings are unreasonable and erroneous in fact and in law. The appellant is indeed at risk and cannot receive adequate protection in Haiti. • The RPD erred in failing to consider all of the evidence and, as a result, its decision lacks justification and intelligibility.

I note that even though the appellant raised the arguments above, he did not support them with specific evidence stating the errors made in the decision and indicating where the problems arose during the hearing.

I note that paragraph 3(3)(g) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules) requires the appellant's memorandum to include full and detailed submissions regarding i. the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, ii. where the errors are located in the written reasons for the RDP's decision that the appellant is appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the RPD's hearing, iii. how any documentary evidence referred to in paragraph (e) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the appellant, iv. the decision the appellant wants the Division to make, and v. why the Division should hold a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the Act if the appellant is requesting that a hearing be held.4

It should be noted that subparagraphs 3(3)(g)(i) and 3(3)(g)(ii) are particularly relevant in this case. I consider that this appeal does not comply with subparagraphs 3(3)(g)(i) and 3(3)(g)(ii) of the RAD Rules because the appellant does not state in the memorandum the sections of the RPD's reasons he considers problematic and does not fully explain why the conclusions are problematic or indicate the specific errors he has identified in that section.

The RAD Rules are clear: the appellant must present a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding the errors that are the grounds of the appeal. In this case, there is an absence or insufficiency of arguments or analysis as to why these issues raised resulted in erroneous findings of fact.

The appeal process is party driven. As Justice LeBlanc states in Dhillon [14]: It is not the RAD's function to supplement the weaknesses of an appeal before it, or, for that matter, of the refugee protection claim presented in the first place. It is not its role to come up with new ideas that might assist appellants in succeeding with their appeal and, ultimately, their refugee claim.

The RAD considers that the requirements of subparagraphs 3(3)(g)(i) and 3(3)(g)(ii) of the RAD Rules are not met. Nevertheless, I conducted an independent assessment of the RPD record, including listening to the recording of the RPD's hearing, and reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted. Credibility

The RPD concluded that the appellant's allegations of harm at the hands of the gangs and the two gang leaders he calls XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX in his birth region in Haiti were not credible for the following reasons: • Omission, in the written account of his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), of the allegation of death threats after he left Haiti. • Inconsistency between his oral evidence and the written account in his BOC Form regarding the threats coming from the XXXX family. • Contradiction about where he learned about the threats previously mentioned. • Lack of a reasonable explanation regarding requests and threats from individuals associated with XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX and the family relationship. • Behaviour inconsistent with his alleged fear of losing his life, as he returned to live in Haiti at the same home in XXXX 2013 after leaving for the United States in XXXX 2013 because he feared for his life in XXXX 2013.

Having reviewed all the evidence, including the documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP), and having listened to the recording of the RPD's hearing, I conclude that there is no significant error in the RPD's decision. The determinative issue is that of the appellant's credibility. At the beginning of the hearing, as is appropriate, the principal appellant was questioned about the truthfulness of the contents of his BOC Form, and he confirmed that the contents were correct. The RPD identified omissions between his testimony and the BOC Form, and the explanations for them were not satisfactory. It gave him every opportunity to provide the necessary clarifications, but he again failed to do so. I therefore consider the RPD's conclusion to be entirely correct: the omission, contradictions and inconsistencies with respect to the death threats undermine the appellant's credibility. I am also of the view that the appellant's actions are inconsistent, in the absence of satisfactory explanations, with the behaviour of someone who is fleeing from his attackers, and this consequently undermines his credibility. After my own analysis of the evidence, I note that the appellant did not apply for asylum during his stay in the United States, even though he testified that he left Haiti in XXXX 2013 because he feared for his life, while considering the fact that he returned to Haiti willingly, which further undermines his credibility.
The RPD correctly analyzed the appellant's credibility. The RPD concluded that the appellant failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

Due to the lack of submissions to address specific errors made by the RPD, and the lack of references to the location of the errors in the RPD decision and/or the audio recording of the hearing, the RAD is not required to go any further. In addition, I note that the appellant is represented by a lawyer who should have a good knowledge of the RAD Rules. I would also point out that there are resources available to appellants and representatives alike to make and prepare their appeals: information sessions on how to appeal to the RAD, and specifically how to perfect an appeal to the RAD, an online Appellant's Record template that sets out all the information that must be provided on appeal, and the Appellant's Guide, which is accessible in 16 languages on the RAD's webpage.

A lack of compliance with RAD Rule 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules leaves the RAD in a position that it must "guess" at the potential errors that the RPD may have committed. As stated in Dhillon, "It is not the RAD's function to supplement the weaknesses of an appeal before it, or, for that matter, of the refugee protection claim presented in the first place. It is also not its role to come up with new ideas that might assist appellants in succeeding with their appeal and, ultimately, their refugee claim."5 Justice Gleeson remarks, in obiter in Ghauri that "... it is the appellant's responsibility, not the RAD's to establish that the RPD erred in a way that justifies the interventions of the RAD."6 The court concluded that "appellants before the RAD that fail to specify where and how the RPD erred do so at their own peril."7

Furthermore, Justice Fothergill states in Murugesu "It is not the RAD's function to supplement the weaknesses of an appeal before it,"8 and in Liu, the Federal Court states that "Rule 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules, SOR/2012-257, places the onus on an appellant to identify in his or her submissions to the RAD the errors that form the grounds of appeal,"9 in addition to the location of the errors in the RPD's decision. In more recent case law, the Courts reiterate the lack of obligation on the part of the RAD to seek out errors made by the RPD. As stated by Chief Justice Crampton in Dahal with respect to RAD Rules 3(3)(g)(i) and (ii):
... In essence, what the RAD did was to briefly review the full record before the RPD, to ensure that it did not make any errors that were not identified by the Applicants.

By simply satisfying itself that no such additional errors were made, the RAD's decision should not become vulnerable to being set aside on judicial review, based solely on its general concurrence with findings made by the RPD in respect of matters that were not raised on appeal by the Applicants. In my view, this would largely vitiate the purpose of Rule 3(3)(g) of the Rules, which requires an appellant to identify (i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal (ii) where those errors are located in the RPD's decision, or in the transcript recording of its hearing.10
In my view, this makes it clear that the RAD is required to focus on the specific errors that an appellant has alleged have been made by the RPD.

I have conducted an independent assessment of all the evidence before the RPD in relation to the errors raised by the appellant. However, having listened to the audio recording of the RPD hearing, I find that the RPD accurately restated the appellant's testimony in this regard. I have also read the NDP with respect to the availability of state protection in Haiti, and I agree with the RPD's credibility assessment.

In light of all the above, I am of the opinion that the appellant did not establish that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he return to Haiti. I also conclude that the appellant did not demonstrate that he faces a serious possibility of persecution on one of the Convention grounds, namely, membership in a particular social group, should he return to Haiti.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the RPD's determination that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
